question: How would you run this for real with a message broker and many workers, and why would you shard by user?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi (honest): ek process, `InMemoryJobQueue` jiska `claim()` O(n) scan hai, restart par sab gaya. Par interface -- claim with lease, `owns`, `complete` / `reschedule` with lease token -- jaan boojh kar SQS / BullMQ / Postgres `SKIP LOCKED` ki shape ka hai. Production design:

1. API tier (stateless, `createApp` jaisa): validate, idempotency check, record DB mein likho, aur job publish -- dono ek saath ho iske liye transactional outbox (record + outbox row ek transaction, ek relay broker ko bhejta hai). Warna record bana par job kho gaya.
2. Broker: SQS / Kafka / RabbitMQ. SQS ka visibility timeout = hamari lease; delay = `runAt` (retries aur quiet hours ke delayed jobs; SQS max 15 min delay hai, lambe deferrals ke liye scheduler table). Priority ke liye do queues (transactional, marketing), workers pehle transactional poll karein.
3. Workers per channel pool: push workers, SMS workers alag scale; har pool ka apna breaker aur provider rate limit.
4. Stores: records / deliveries DB, idempotency keys Redis (TTL 24 h), caps Redis (ratelimit-kit ka store), inbox wide-column / Postgres.

Shard by user kyun? Kyunki is system ka almost har invariant per-user hai: frequency caps per user, quiet hours per user, token list per user, inbox aur unread counter per user, idempotency per request-of-a-user. Same user ke jobs ek partition (Kafka key = user_id) par jaayein toh ordering aur contention ek jagah, cross-shard transaction kabhi nahi chahiye. Hot user (celebrity nahi, par bot jo spam trigger kare) ek partition ko garam karta hai -- per-user rate limit API par.
why_needed: HLD round ka core: in-memory LLD ko durable, horizontally scalable system mein kaise badlein bina guarantees khoye.
real_world_analogy: Ek dukaan se chain of stores: har store apne area ke customers (shard by user) sambhalta hai, central godown (broker) maal bhejta hai, aur har order ki entry pehle register (outbox) mein hoti hai.
how_it_works: Request -> API (validate + DB write + outbox) -> relay -> broker partition(user_id) -> channel worker (lease = visibility timeout) -> provider -> result DB mein lease/version check ke saath.
in_this_project: Code ke seams: `src/queue.ts` ka `JobQueue` interface (`owns`, `complete`, `reschedule` with lease token), `src/users.ts::UserDirectory` ("in a real system this is another service or a table"), `src/senders.ts::ChannelSender` (real provider = one more class). README stage 2 'known and NOT handled': in memory, one process, `claim()` O(n), worker batches. Sab production pieces NOT built.
advantages: Interface already broker-shaped, swap localized
Per-user sharding = no cross-shard transactions
Channel pools independently scale
disadvantages: Outbox, relay, scheduler -- moving parts badhte hain
Broker-specific limits (SQS 15 min delay, FIFO throughput limits)
Lease ab do jagah (broker visibility + DB version)
common_mistakes: DB write aur publish ko bina outbox ke alag karna (dual write)
Visibility timeout ko send timeout se chhota rakhna
Shard key notification id rakhna (per-user invariants bikhar jaate)
follow_up_questions: How does the transactional outbox avoid the dual-write problem?
How would you handle a deferral longer than the broker's max delay?
What happens to strict priority starvation with two queues?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Kafka: ordering per partition, replay, high throughput -- par per-message delay / visibility nahi, retries ke liye retry topics. SQS: visibility timeout aur delay built-in (hamare model se seedha match), ordering weak. Postgres SKIP LOCKED: simple, transactional with records, par scale limit. Main chhote-medium scale par Postgres jobs, bade par SQS ya Kafka + retry topics recommend karunga.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Relay down -> outbox rows jama, notifications late par lost nahi. Worker crash -> visibility timeout -> redelivery -> provider idempotency key + DB lease/version check (S22 lesson). Broker partition hot -> ek user ke jobs late, baaki unaffected.
advanced.alternatives: Managed services (AWS SNS / Pinpoint, Firebase) ya vendors (Courier, Knock) jo yeh poori pipeline dete hain -- build vs buy. Event-driven: domain events (OrderShipped) se notification service subscribe kare.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x: zyada workers per channel, DB read replicas. 100x: user-sharded DB aur broker partitions, region-local pipelines, provider multicast, aur per-channel autoscaling queue depth par.
advanced.production_improvements: Queue depth aur age metrics per priority, DLQ for poison jobs, outbox lag alert, aging for marketing starvation (README: not built), aur canary workers for provider adapter changes.

question: Providers impose rate limits and you need to run in several regions. How would you extend this design?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein dono NAHI hain: fakes ki koi rate limit nahi, aur sab ek process ek region mein. Jo hai woh per-user marketing frequency cap (ratelimit-kit) aur per-channel circuit breaker aur timeout (resilience-kit). Production extension:

Provider rate limits: FCM, APNs, Twilio, SES sab per-account / per-second limits lagaate hain aur over-limit par 429 dete hain. (1) Ek GLOBAL per-provider limiter (token bucket, shared store jaise Redis) jo worker call se pehle token le -- user cap se alag cheez, yeh hamare poore account ka throughput hai. (2) Token na mile toh job ko delay ke saath reschedule karo, attempt jalaaye bina -- bilkul circuit-open "all" path jaisa (no call made = no attempt). (3) 429 ko retryable maano, `Retry-After` respect karo, aur use breaker failure count mat banao, kyunki provider healthy hai, hum fast hain. (4) Priority: transactional ke liye limit ka reserved hissa (OTP marketing blast ke peeche na atke). SMS ke liye per-country / per-sender-number limits bhi hote hain.

Multi-region: user ka "home region" -- uske records, inbox, tokens, caps wahin. Sharding by user ka natural extension. API kisi bhi region mein aaye toh home region ko forward. Kyun? Caps aur idempotency per user hain; do regions independently cap check karein toh user ko double marketing; idempotency key do regions mein toh duplicate OTP. Region failover par: home region ki data replicated (async) standby mein, failover ke baad thode duplicates possible -- provider idempotency keys (`<id>:push:<token>`) unhe kam karti hain. Providers ke regional endpoints aur data-residency rules (EU data EU mein) bhi home region tay karte hain.
why_needed: Real providers ka throughput limited hai aur users globally hain; bina iske ek marketing blast OTPs ko rok sakta hai ya ek region outage poora system.
real_world_analogy: Toll plaza par lanes limited hain (provider limit): VIP lane (transactional) alag rakho, aur har city ka apna depot (home region) ho taaki ek city band ho toh poora desh na ruke.
how_it_works: Worker: global limiter token -> mila toh call, nahi mila toh reschedule without attempt. 429 -> retryable with Retry-After. Region: request -> home region routing -> region-local pipeline.
in_this_project: Existing pieces: `src/queued-notifier.ts` (frequency cap ratelimit-kit se, marketing only, first try only; cap store down -> job waits; circuit-open 'all' path bina attempt ke reschedule), README stage 2 rules table. Global provider limiter, 429 handling aur multi-region -- NOT built.
advantages: Provider ka throughput respect, account ban se bachaav
Transactional ke liye reserved capacity
Home region se per-user invariants simple
disadvantages: Shared limiter store ek aur dependency (down ho toh? -- cap store jaisa 'wait' rule)
Multi-region failover par duplicates aur data lag
common_mistakes: 429 ko permanent failure maanna
429 ko breaker failure count karna aur circuit khol dena
Har region mein independently caps aur idempotency check karna
follow_up_questions: What should happen when the shared limiter store is down?
How do you split provider capacity between transactional and marketing?
What duplicates can happen during a region failover, and how do you limit them?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Global limiter centralized hai (Redis) -- accurate par ek hot key; alternative: har worker ko quota ka hissa (local token bucket, limit / N) -- no shared store par uneven. Home-region model consistency simple rakhta hai, active-active writes conflict laate.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Marketing blast provider limit kha jaaye -> OTP late: isliye reserved capacity. Limiter store down -> 'wait' (cap store jaisa) ya local fallback quota. Region down -> standby promote, async replication lag ke messages dobara ho sakte hain; idempotency keys provider side par kuch bachate hain.
advanced.alternatives: Provider ka multicast / batch API (FCM multiple tokens, SES bulk) calls kam karta hai; multiple provider accounts / vendors for failover (Twilio + doosra SMS vendor) -- naya ChannelSender aur 'first' mode ki tarah vendor fallback.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x: global limiter shard per provider account. 100x: multiple provider accounts per region, region-local limiters, aur marketing sends ko off-peak schedule karna.
advanced.production_improvements: 429 rate aur limiter wait time ke dashboards, per-country SMS limits, data-residency based home region, aur game days (region failover drills).

question: What breaks first at 10x and 100x traffic, in the device fan-out and the inbox, and what would you change?
answer_hinglish:
Pehle: is project mein koi benchmark ya latency number nahi hai, toh yeh reasoning hai, measurement nahi.

In-memory version mein jo pehle tootega: `InMemoryJobQueue.claim()` har job scan karta hai (O(n), README mein documented) -- backlog badhte hi har claim mehenga. Worker batches mein chalta hai (sabse slow job ka wait), toh ek slow device poore batch ko rokta hai. Records kabhi remove nahi hote aur `sentBy` index trim nahi hota -- memory badhti rehti hai. Ek process = ek CPU core ki limit.

Device fan-out at scale: provider calls = notifications x devices (cap 10, typically 1-3). 10x par per-provider rate limits pehle hit honge. Fix: provider multicast APIs (ek request kai tokens -- not built), per-channel worker pools, aur `Promise.all` ki jagah har device ka result jaise aaye waise process (ek slow tablet phone ki delivery na roke). Dead token cleanup scale par important ho jaata hai -- warna stale tokens calls ka bada hissa ban jaate.

Inbox at scale: writes = har in_app notification (broadcast mein lakhon users ko ek saath). Reads = har app open par unread count. Stored counter O(1) read deta hai; page query keyset hai (O(log n + limit)). 100x par: inbox ek wide-column store (partition user_id, cluster seq DESC) ya user-sharded Postgres, unread count Redis cache mein, retention 200 per user storage bound rakhta hai (users x 200 x item size). Broadcast fan-out-on-write mehenga ho toh "global announcements" ko fan-out-on-read (ek shared item + per-user read marker).

Real-time: abhi app poll karti hai (count endpoint). 100x par polling load bada -- WebSocket / SSE push (not built) ya long-poll with ETag.
why_needed: Senior round mein interviewer dekhta hai ki tum bottlenecks order mein pehchante ho aur har ek ka targeted fix bata sakte ho, bina numbers invent kiye.
real_world_analogy: Shaadi ke invitations: 50 guests ko haath se de sakte ho, 5000 ke liye courier company (broker), aur sabko ek hi notice ke liye mandap ke bahar ek board (fan-out-on-read).
how_it_works: Bottleneck chain: claim scan -> batch worker -> provider limits -> fan-out calls -> inbox writes -> count reads / polling.
in_this_project: README: "claim() scans every job (O(n))", "The worker runs in batches", "Records are never removed", receipts "the provider-index (sentBy) is never trimmed", devices "Not built: ... the provider's own multicast API", inbox "Not built: a real-time push of new items to an open app (WebSocket / SSE; the app polls the count)". `src/inbox.ts` page binary search aur stored `unread`; `src/users.ts` `MAX_PUSH_TOKENS = 10`.
advantages: Bounded per-user data (10 tokens, 200 items) scale ko predictable banata hai
O(1) count aur keyset paging pehle se scale-friendly
Seams (JobQueue, UserDirectory, ChannelSender) swap ke liye ready
disadvantages: In-memory queue aur records 10x par hi toot jaate
Fan-out calls devices ke multiple mein
Polling inbox load
common_mistakes: Bina measurement ke numbers bolna
Fan-out-on-write ko broadcast ke liye bhi use karna
Sirf workers badhana jab provider limit asli bottleneck ho
follow_up_questions: How would you decide between fan-out-on-write and fan-out-on-read for the inbox?
Which metric tells you the provider, not your workers, is the bottleneck?
How would you load-test this without real providers?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Fan-out-on-write (har user ka item) reads sasta, broadcast writes mehenga; fan-out-on-read ulta. Mix: personal notifications on-write, announcements on-read. Per-device parallel calls latency kam, provider load zyada; multicast dono ka beech.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Backlog spike -> O(n) claim -> workers slow -> leases expire -> duplicates (at-least-once) -> aur load. Ek slow provider -> batch worker ke saare slots wait. Broadcast -> inbox write storm -> counter updates hot.
advanced.alternatives: Kafka partitions + per-channel consumers; provider multicast; Redis for counts; CDN-like edge for inbox reads nahi (personal data) par read replicas haan.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x: broker + DB + worker pools + records retention. 100x: user sharding, region-local pipelines, multicast, fan-out-on-read for broadcasts, WebSocket gateway for real-time inbox.
advanced.production_improvements: Load test with fake providers jo configurable latency / 429 / errors dein (FakeSender ka script idea scale par), queue depth / age / leaseLost / provider-latency SLOs, aur capacity plan har channel ke provider limit se peeche ki taraf.
